objectives: Trace philosophy from Socrates + Plato + Aristotle + Stoics + Epicurus through the medieval + modern canon.
Map the early-modern + Enlightenment turn — Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, Hume, Kant, Hegel.
Survey the 20th-century split between analytic (Frege + Russell + Wittgenstein + Quine) + continental (Husserl + Heidegger + Sartre + Foucault + Derrida) traditions.

slides.title: Ancient philosophy: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Stoics, Epicurus
slides.body:
**Philosophy** = systematic inquiry into the most general + foundational questions about reality (metaphysics), knowledge (epistemology), value (ethics + aesthetics + politics), and reasoning (logic). Its written history begins ~600 BCE in the Greek world + parallel traditions in India + China.

**Pre-Socratics**: Thales, Anaximander, Heraclitus (*panta rhei*, the logos), Parmenides (being is one + unchanging), Pythagoras, Democritus (atomism), Empedocles. They posed the cosmological + ontological questions that would set the agenda.

**Socrates (470-399 BCE)**: wrote nothing himself; we know him through Plato + Xenophon + Aristophanes. The **Socratic method** (*elenchus*) — relentless dialectical questioning exposing contradiction + ignorance. 'The unexamined life is not worth living' (*Apology*). Insisted on the priority of ethical knowledge ('virtue is knowledge'; moral intellectualism). Executed by Athens 399 BCE for impiety + corrupting the youth — the founding martyrdom of philosophy.

**Plato (428-348 BCE)**: founded the Academy ~387 BCE. Wrote dialogues (~35 surviving): *Apology*, *Meno*, *Phaedo*, *Symposium*, *Phaedrus*, *Theaetetus*, *Sophist*, *Timaeus*.
- ***Republic*** (~375 BCE): theory of justice as harmony of soul + city; the **Allegory of the Cave** (Book VII) — prisoners take shadows for reality; **the Divided Line** + **theory of Forms** (eternal, unchanging, intelligible objects of knowledge; particulars *participate* in Forms); the philosopher-king; the tripartite soul (reason, spirit, appetite); critique of poetry + democracy.
- The Forms make universals real + epistemology possible: knowledge (*epistēmē*) is of Forms; opinion (*doxa*) is of particulars.
- Whitehead: 'the safest general characterization of the European philosophical tradition is that it consists of a series of footnotes to Plato.'

**Aristotle (384-322 BCE)**: Plato's student; tutored Alexander; founded the Lyceum 335 BCE. Encyclopedic — logic, physics, biology, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric, poetics. The first systematic logician (syllogistic).
- ***Nicomachean Ethics***: ethics as the study of human flourishing (*eudaimonia*); virtue (*aretē*) as a stable disposition to feel + act well; the **doctrine of the mean** (courage between cowardice + rashness); practical wisdom (*phronēsis*); friendship; the contemplative life.
- ***Metaphysics***: substance + form + matter + the four causes (material, formal, efficient, final); potentiality + actuality; the unmoved mover.
- ***Politics***: humans as political animals; constitutions; the polis.
- ***Organon*** + ***Posterior Analytics***: term logic; demonstration; first principles.
Aristotle's empirical + teleological + systematic style dominated Western thought for two millennia.

**Hellenistic schools** (after Alexander): philosophy as therapy for living.
- **Stoics** (Zeno of Citium ~300 BCE; Chrysippus; Epictetus *Discourses* + *Enchiridion*; Seneca *Letters*; Marcus Aurelius *Meditations*): virtue is the only good; live according to nature + reason (*logos*); the dichotomy of control (*ta eph' hēmin*) — focus on what is up to you, accept what isn't; *apatheia* — freedom from destructive passion. Foundation of CBT-style cognitive reframing 2300 years later.
- **Epicurus (341-270 BCE)**: pleasure (*hēdonē*) — properly understood as absence of pain (*aponia*) + tranquility (*ataraxia*) — is the good; atomism inherited from Democritus; gods exist but don't interfere; death is nothing to us. *Letter to Menoeceus*; Lucretius *De Rerum Natura* (~50 BCE).
- **Skeptics** (Pyrrho; Sextus Empiricus *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*): suspend judgment (*epochē*) → tranquility.
- **Cynics** (Diogenes): radical rejection of convention.
- **Neoplatonism** (Plotinus *Enneads* ~3rd c. CE): the One, Nous, Soul — bridge to Christianity + Islamic philosophy.

slides.title: Medieval + early-modern: Augustine, Aquinas, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, Hume, Kant, Hegel
slides.body:
**Medieval philosophy** wove Greek thought into Abrahamic theology — Christian, Islamic, Jewish.

**Augustine of Hippo (354-430)**: *Confessions* (~400) — the first introspective autobiography + theology of the will + time (Book XI). *City of God* (413-426). Inner self, original sin, divine illumination, predestination, just war. Pivot from Plato to Christian Neoplatonism.

**Islamic philosophy** (huge in its own right): **al-Kindi**, **al-Farabi**, **Avicenna (Ibn Sina)** *The Book of Healing* + *Canon of Medicine*, **al-Ghazali** *Incoherence of the Philosophers*, **Averroes (Ibn Rushd)** Aristotle commentaries — transmitted + extended Greek philosophy into Latin Europe via 12th-13th c. translation movements (Toledo).

**Jewish philosophy**: **Maimonides** *Guide for the Perplexed* (~1190) — reconciling Aristotle + Torah.

**Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274)**: Dominican; *Summa Theologiae* + *Summa contra Gentiles* — the great Christian synthesis of Aristotle + Augustine. **Five Ways** for God's existence (motion, causation, contingency, gradation, teleology). Natural law ethics. Faith + reason as compatible domains. Canonical theologian of the Catholic Church.

Late-medieval + Renaissance — **Duns Scotus**, **William of Ockham** (Ockham's razor; nominalism), Renaissance humanism, **Machiavelli** (*The Prince* 1513).

**Early-modern rationalism**:
- **René Descartes (1596-1650)**: ***Meditations on First Philosophy*** (1641). Methodic doubt → *cogito, ergo sum* (I think, therefore I am) — the indubitable Archimedean point. Mind-body dualism (res cogitans + res extensa). The pineal gland. Cartesian coordinates + analytic geometry. The 'father of modern philosophy.'
- **Baruch Spinoza (1632-1677)**: ***Ethics*** (posthumous 1677), geometric-method *more geometrico*. Pantheism — God = Nature (*Deus sive Natura*); substance monism; necessitarianism; the conatus; intellectual love of God; toleration + biblical criticism (*Theological-Political Treatise* 1670). Excommunicated by Amsterdam's Jewish community; rediscovered + canonized later.
- **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716)**: ***Monadology*** (1714); pre-established harmony; the principle of sufficient reason; possible worlds (this is the best of all); calculus (independent of Newton); identity of indiscernibles. *Discourse on Metaphysics*; *Theodicy* (1710).

**British empiricism**:
- **John Locke (1632-1704)**: ***Essay Concerning Human Understanding*** (1689) — the mind as *tabula rasa*; ideas come from sensation + reflection; primary vs secondary qualities; substance + identity (Locke on persons). *Two Treatises of Government* (1689) — natural rights + consent + property — foundation of liberalism. *A Letter Concerning Toleration*.
- **George Berkeley (1685-1753)**: *esse est percipi* — to be is to be perceived; idealism.
- **David Hume (1711-1776)**: ***A Treatise of Human Nature*** (1739-40); ***Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding*** (1748). Causation is constant conjunction + custom, not necessity (problem of induction); the bundle theory of self; the *is-ought* gap; mitigated skepticism; miracles; the natural history of religion. The hinge of Anglophone empiricism.

**Immanuel Kant (1724-1804)**: ***Critique of Pure Reason*** (1781; 2nd ed. 1787) — the *Copernican revolution* of philosophy: objects conform to the mind's structure, not vice versa. **Synthetic a priori** judgments (mathematics, the laws of physics); the categories (substance, causation, etc.) as conditions of possible experience; **phenomena** (things as they appear) vs **noumena** (things in themselves). Critique of the four classical metaphysical errors (paralogisms + antinomies). ***Critique of Practical Reason*** (1788) + ***Groundwork for the Metaphysics of Morals*** (1785) — the **categorical imperative** (act only on maxims you could will as universal law; treat humanity as end in itself, not mere means); autonomy; the kingdom of ends. ***Critique of Judgment*** (1790) — aesthetics + teleology. *Perpetual Peace* (1795). Kant's three Critiques restructure all subsequent philosophy.

**German idealism**: **Fichte**, **Schelling**, **G. W. F. Hegel (1770-1831)** — ***Phenomenology of Spirit*** (1807); ***Science of Logic*** (1812-1816); ***Philosophy of Right*** (1820). The dialectic (thesis-antithesis-synthesis is a later schematic); *Geist* (spirit) actualizing itself through history; recognition; the master-slave dialectic; the cunning of reason. **Schopenhauer** (the will), **Kierkegaard** (existential individual), **Marx** (turned Hegel on his head), **Nietzsche** (genealogy + revaluation) all stand in Hegel's wake.

slides.title: 20th-century split: analytic (Frege + Russell + Wittgenstein + Quine) vs continental (Husserl + Heidegger + Sartre + Foucault + Derrida)
slides.body:
Around 1900 a methodological split opened that still organizes the discipline.

**Analytic philosophy** — emerges from the logical revolution.
- **Gottlob Frege (1848-1925)**: ***Begriffsschrift*** (1879) — modern predicate logic with quantifiers; the foundations of arithmetic in logic (*Grundgesetze* 1893-1903 — derailed by **Russell's paradox**). **Sense + reference** (*Sinn und Bedeutung* 1892): the morning star = the evening star; same reference, different sense. Foundation of philosophy of language + analytic semantics.
- **Bertrand Russell (1872-1970)**: with **Alfred North Whitehead** wrote ***Principia Mathematica*** (1910-1913) — three-volume reduction of mathematics to logic (logicism); discovered Russell's paradox (the set of all sets that aren't members of themselves). ***On Denoting*** (1905) — theory of definite descriptions ('the present king of France is bald'). Logical atomism. *History of Western Philosophy* (1945). Nobel Prize in Literature 1950.
- **Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889-1951)**: ***Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*** (1921) — the world is the totality of facts; language pictures facts; 'whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' Later — ***Philosophical Investigations*** (posthumous 1953) — **language games**; meaning as use; rule-following; the private-language argument; family resemblance. Repudiated his own *Tractatus*; reshaped 20th-century philosophy twice.
- **Vienna Circle + logical positivism** (Schlick, Carnap, Neurath, Hempel, Ayer): the verification principle — meaningful statements are either analytic or empirically verifiable. Famously self-undermining + dismantled by Quine.
- **W. V. O. Quine (1908-2000)**: ***Two Dogmas of Empiricism*** (1951) — rejects the analytic-synthetic distinction + reductionism; meaning is holistic; the **web of belief**. *Word and Object* (1960) — indeterminacy of translation; ontological commitment ('to be is to be the value of a bound variable'). Naturalized epistemology.
- **Saul Kripke** (*Naming and Necessity* 1972), **Donald Davidson** (truth-conditional semantics + anomalous monism), **Hilary Putnam** (Twin Earth + content externalism + internal realism), **John Rawls** (lesson 7), **Derek Parfit** (*Reasons and Persons* 1984), **David Lewis** (modal realism — lesson 4), **Saul Kripke + Putnam + Burge** (semantic externalism) push the analytic tradition into metaphysics + ethics + mind.

**Continental philosophy** — phenomenology, existentialism, hermeneutics, structuralism, post-structuralism.
- **Edmund Husserl (1859-1938)**: founder of **phenomenology**. *Logical Investigations* (1900-01); ***Ideas*** (1913); *Cartesian Meditations* (1931); *Crisis of European Sciences* (1936). Bracket (*epochē*) the natural attitude; describe the structures of intentional consciousness. 'To the things themselves.'
- **Martin Heidegger (1889-1976)**: ***Being and Time*** (1927) — the question of being (*Seinsfrage*); *Dasein* (the entity that asks about being); being-in-the-world; thrownness; being-toward-death; the ontological difference; later turn — language, technology, *Gelassenheit*. Politically compromised (Nazi party 1933) — a permanent ethical stain.
- **Jean-Paul Sartre (1905-1980)**: ***Being and Nothingness*** (1943); ***Existentialism Is a Humanism*** (1946). Existence precedes essence; radical freedom; bad faith; the look; nausea. Existentialism — Kierkegaard + Heidegger + Sartre + Camus + de Beauvoir (***The Second Sex*** 1949 — foundational text of modern feminist philosophy). **Maurice Merleau-Ponty** *Phenomenology of Perception* (1945) — embodied phenomenology.
- **Hermeneutics**: **Gadamer** *Truth and Method* (1960); **Ricoeur** *Time and Narrative*. The hermeneutic circle.
- **Structuralism + post-structuralism**: **Saussure** (linguistics), **Lévi-Strauss** (anthropology), **Roland Barthes**, **Jacques Lacan** (psychoanalysis).
- **Michel Foucault (1926-1984)**: archaeology + genealogy. ***Madness and Civilization*** (1961); ***The Order of Things*** (1966); ***Discipline and Punish*** (1975); ***History of Sexuality*** (1976+). Power/knowledge; biopower; governmentality; the panopticon.
- **Jacques Derrida (1930-2004)**: ***Of Grammatology*** (1967); *Writing and Difference* (1967); *Margins of Philosophy*. **Deconstruction**; *différance*; logocentrism; the metaphysics of presence. Polarizing — analytic philosophers often hostile.
- **Frankfurt School** (lesson 7): Horkheimer, Adorno (*Dialectic of Enlightenment* 1947), Marcuse, Habermas.

**Reconvergence (1990s+)**: the analytic-continental divide has narrowed — **Brandom** (Hegelian pragmatism), **McDowell** (Kantian-Wittgensteinian), Putnam, **Bernard Williams** (lesson 5), Korsgaard. **Anglophone metaethics**, **moral psychology**, **philosophy of mind + cognitive science** (lesson 6), **political philosophy** (lesson 7), **AI ethics + experimental philosophy** (lesson 8) are now substantially integrated. The rest of this Philosopher path develops the threads: logic + language (2), epistemology (3), metaphysics (4), ethics (5), mind (6), politics (7), modern frontier (8).

question.question: Reason through Kant's Copernican revolution + its consequences
question.goal: Show why Kant's claim that *objects conform to the mind* — not the mind to objects — restructured all subsequent philosophy.

steps.prompt: What problem did Kant inherit from Hume?

acceptedAnswers: hume's skeptical argument that causation + induction + the self lack rational justification; we have only custom + habit

steps.reveal: Hume (1739-1748) argued: (1) causation isn't observed — we see only constant conjunction + feel custom expecting B after A; (2) induction lacks rational justification — past regularities don't entail future ones; (3) the self isn't observed — only a bundle of perceptions. This 'awakened me from my dogmatic slumber' (Kant 1783). If Hume is right, science + metaphysics + the unified self are illusions.

acceptedAnswers: objects conform to the structure of the mind (categories + forms of intuition), not the mind to objects — making synthetic a priori knowledge possible

steps.reveal: Kant inverted the relation: instead of asking how the mind grasps an independently structured world, ask what the mind *imposes* on experience to make experience possible at all. Space + time are **forms of intuition** (we cannot experience without them). **Categories of understanding** (substance, causation, unity, plurality, etc.) are the rules by which the mind unifies appearances. They are *necessary preconditions* of any possible experience — hence **synthetic a priori**. Causation isn't read off the world; it is the world (as we can know it) made coherent.

acceptedAnswers: we know phenomena (things as they appear to us, structured by the categories) but not noumena (things in themselves); traditional metaphysics of soul, world, god overreaches

steps.reveal: We know **phenomena** — appearances structured by the forms + categories. We do not know **noumena** — things in themselves, as they are independent of our cognitive structure. Traditional metaphysics — proofs of the soul's immortality, of God's existence, of the world as finite or infinite — generates antinomies + paralogisms precisely because it tries to extend the categories beyond possible experience. The *Transcendental Dialectic* maps these errors. Metaphysics becomes critique.

steps.prompt: What follows for ethics + the Critiques to come?

acceptedAnswers: the categorical imperative + autonomy + kingdom of ends in the second critique; aesthetics + teleology in the third — together restructuring epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics

steps.reveal: If knowledge is limited to phenomena, metaphysical claims about freedom + God + immortality cannot be proven theoretically — but practical reason (the moral law) requires them as postulates. The **categorical imperative** (act only on maxims you could will as universal law; treat humanity always also as an end) follows from autonomy — being a rational agent legislating universally. The third *Critique* (1790) extends to aesthetic judgment + teleology — bridging nature + freedom. Kant's three Critiques restructured epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, + aesthetics in a single architectonic — every subsequent philosopher (Hegel, Husserl, Frege, Wittgenstein, Quine, Rawls, Korsgaard) negotiates with Kant.

question.question: Why is the analytic-continental split a defining feature of 20th-century philosophy?
options: Around 1900 two methodological traditions diverged. The **analytic tradition** (Frege 1879 *Begriffsschrift*; Russell + Whitehead 1910-13 *Principia Mathematica*; early Wittgenstein 1921 *Tractatus*; Vienna Circle; Quine 1951 *Two Dogmas*; Kripke 1972 *Naming and Necessity*) prioritized formal logic, conceptual analysis, clarity, philosophy of language + science + mind. The **continental tradition** (Husserl 1900-13 phenomenology; Heidegger 1927 *Being and Time*; Sartre 1943 *Being and Nothingness*; Foucault 1975 *Discipline and Punish*; Derrida 1967 *Of Grammatology*) prioritized phenomenology, historical + cultural critique, hermeneutics, structuralism + post-structuralism. The two split on style (logical formalism vs. close textual + historical reading), canon (Frege-Russell-Wittgenstein-Quine-Kripke vs. Hegel-Nietzsche-Husserl-Heidegger-Foucault-Derrida), institutions (Anglophone vs. French + German), + questions (truth + reference + mind vs. being + power + difference). Mutual hostility was real (Carnap on Heidegger; analytic reception of Derrida) but has narrowed since the 1990s — Brandom, McDowell, Putnam, Williams + Korsgaard + Habermas dialogue across the line. The split shaped curricula, hiring, journals + the discipline's self-image for a century.
question.explanation: Analytic (Frege 1879; Russell + Whitehead 1910-13; Wittgenstein 1921 + 1953; Vienna Circle; Quine 1951; Kripke 1972) prioritized logic + conceptual analysis + philosophy of language / science / mind. Continental (Husserl; Heidegger 1927; Sartre 1943; Foucault; Derrida 1967) prioritized phenomenology + hermeneutics + cultural critique + structuralism / post-structuralism. Reconverging since 1990s via Brandom, McDowell, Putnam, Williams + Habermas.

slides.workedSolution: Analytic (Frege 1879; Russell + Whitehead Principia 1910-13; Wittgenstein 1921 + 1953; Vienna Circle; Quine 1951; Kripke 1972) emphasized formal logic + conceptual analysis + philosophy of language / science / mind. Continental (Husserl; Heidegger 1927; Sartre 1943; Foucault; Derrida 1967) emphasized phenomenology + hermeneutics + cultural critique. The split has narrowed since the 1990s (Brandom, McDowell, Putnam, Williams).

question.question: Tracing one question across traditions
question.prompt: A first-year philosophy student asks: 'What is the self?' Draft a ≤220-word reply that takes them through (a) Plato's tripartite soul (*Republic*) + Aristotle's hylomorphism (*De Anima*); (b) Descartes's cogito (*Meditations* 1641) + Locke's psychological-continuity account; (c) Hume's bundle theory (1739) + Kant's transcendental unity of apperception (1781); (d) Heidegger's *Dasein* (*Being and Time* 1927) + Sartre's radical freedom (1943); + (e) the modern analytic engagement (Parfit *Reasons and Persons* 1984 — psychological continuity + reductionism; Korsgaard *Self-Constitution* — practical-agency view). Identify two specific empirical questions a 21st-century philosopher might investigate (e.g., split-brain cases, narrative identity, neural-correlates work).

question.question: Aristotle organized his ethical analysis around the **doctrine of the mean**. If a virtue $V$ is the mean between a deficiency $D$ and an excess $E$ on some scale, and Aristotle places courage at $V = 5$ on a 0-10 scale with cowardice at $D = 1$ + rashness at $E = 9$, what is the average of $D$ and $E$? Give your answer to one decimal place.
question.hint: $(1 + 9) / 2 = 5.0$. Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* II.6 — virtue is a *mean between two vices*, one of excess + one of deficiency. The mean is not strictly arithmetic; it is *relative to us* + determined by practical wisdom (*phronēsis*). But the arithmetic intuition captures the structural idea — courage between cowardice + rashness, generosity between stinginess + prodigality, etc.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, characterize philosophy as a discipline by naming (a) one core contribution from each of Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, Epicurus; (b) Augustine, Aquinas, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, Hume, Kant, Hegel; (c) Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Quine (analytic) + Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, Foucault, Derrida (continental).
question.rubric: Mentions: Socrates (elenchus + ethical priority + 'unexamined life'); Plato (theory of Forms + *Republic* + Allegory of the Cave); Aristotle (*Nicomachean Ethics* + eudaimonia + doctrine of the mean + four causes + syllogistic); Stoics (dichotomy of control + virtue + apatheia); Epicurus (atomism + ataraxia + 'death is nothing to us'). Augustine (*Confessions* + will + time); Aquinas (*Summa* + five ways + natural law); Descartes (*Meditations* 1641 + cogito + dualism); Spinoza (*Ethics* + Deus sive Natura); Leibniz (monads + possible worlds + PSR); Locke (*Essay* 1689 + tabula rasa + *Two Treatises*); Hume (*Treatise* 1739 + induction + is-ought + bundle theory); Kant (*Critique of Pure Reason* 1781 + Copernican revolution + categorical imperative); Hegel (*Phenomenology* 1807 + dialectic + Geist). Frege (*Begriffsschrift* 1879 + sense/reference); Russell + Whitehead (*Principia* 1910-13); Wittgenstein (*Tractatus* 1921 + *Investigations* 1953 + language games); Quine (1951 *Two Dogmas* + holism). Husserl (phenomenology); Heidegger (*Being and Time* 1927 + Dasein); Sartre (1943 + existence precedes essence); Foucault (1975 *Discipline and Punish* + power/knowledge); Derrida (1967 + deconstruction + différance). Concludes that philosophy is the systematic inquiry into the most general questions about reality, knowledge, value, + reasoning — through reasoned argument across traditions.
